Research (published August 13, 2025) notes many advisors avoid discussing fees upfront, creating an opportunity for transparent advisors; recommended practices include website fee pages, addressing pricing within the first 10 minutes of initial consultations, and providing clear written fee estimates. Why it might matter: the same passage notes that while professional certifications provide objective credibility, many advisors do not effectively communicate their value to prospects.

The broader debate over cash sweep transparency and pricing (trade press, published September 30, 2026) remains a live issue, with the question of who benefits from rising rates on uninvested cash unlikely to fade from client conversations; advisors should be prepared to explain how their custodian's sweep structure works. Why it might matter: the same trade-press passage advises that advisors should be prepared to explain how their custodian's sweep structure works and how it may shift with the rate environment.

Raymond James (10-Q for the quarter ended December 31, 2025) states it has sought to continue to meet client demand for higher yields on cash balances, without sacrificing FDIC insurance benefits, by providing FDIC-insured deposit products and enhanced-rate initiatives. Why it might matter: in the same passage Raymond James notes such programs include its Enhanced Savings Program, where deposits are held by Raymond James Bank.

Trade press (published October 2, 2026) reports that now that clients can make a decent return on cash again, firms realize they must tread carefully when it comes to paying appropriate interest rates to clients on their cash. Why it might matter: trade press notes the SEC's sustained focus on sweep disclosures combined with litigation against firms over low client yields keeps the question of who benefits from rising rates on uninvested cash a live issue.

The comparison of which firms are leading or lagging on fee structure changes and transparency cannot be made on this evidence: the cited items are heterogeneous, spanning different quantities, periods, and scopes with no shared basis or shared periods across firms. Some items concern data-fee introduction timing (trade press reports Charles Schwab introduced data fees over seven years ago, UBS in the mid-2010s, and Merrill Lynch later than many peers), others concern data-fee rate levels (Morgan Stanley between $25,000 and $500,000 versus Merrill's $125,000 to $860,000), and still others concern regulatory settlements of differing amounts and dates (Charles Schwab $187 million in 2022, Raymond James $13 million in July 2023, Wells Fargo and Merrill $4.4 million, Edward Jones $320,754.72 per state), so no valid ranking of firms as leading or lagging can be constructed from this evidence.
